source.title: Large-Scale Language Model Rescoring on Long-Form Data
source.authors: Tongzhou Chen; Cyril Allauzen; Yinghui Huang; Daniel S. Park; David Rybach; W. R. Huang; Rodrigo Cabrera; Kartik Audhkhasi; B. Ramabhadran; Pedro J. Moreno; M. Riley

record.file_problem: Full paper text is provided. Some table formatting is flattened, making Table 5's individual values difficult to assign.
record.tranche_reason: The paper extends evaluation of language-model scaling to long-form ASR rescoring and reports downstream WER at multiple LM sizes, but does not test pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports ASR WER and salient-term error-rate outcomes for language-model rescoring. Table 2's lattice-quality results and Table 3's context-length comparison do not test scale-related predictability. Table 5's flattened layout does not support confident assignment of its values to individual MT5 variants, so those values are not extracted. The conventional neural LM, MaxEnt LM, and combined-fusion results are comparisons rather than separate LLM size-sweep results.
record.test_reason: Table 4 sweeps LM size within T5 (60M–11B) and PaLM (8B–540B) and reports downstream ASR rescoring WER, and the authors note larger T5 gives better results. This bears on V6 qualitatively in a new setting. No curve is fitted and no prediction is made.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors also state that increasing T5 size gives better results and that PaLM beats T5. They attribute smaller en-in gains to the small WEBDOC corpus, citing data-hungry scaling laws.
record.recipe_differences: The paper rescoring-evaluates pretrained and fine-tuned LMs on long-form ASR; it does not fit language-model loss scaling laws or compute-optimal allocation curves.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports that carrying previous-segment context improves over no context, while carrying two segments gives no additional gain over one segment (Table 3). It also reports that WEBDOC fine-tuning improves MT5 rescoring in the code-switching setting, but Table 5's flattened values cannot be assigned confidently.
record.peer_reviewed: IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing, 2023
record.problems: No uncertainty estimates are reported. The downstream evaluation is specific to long-form ASR and does not test loss-law fits or prediction accuracy. The paper's conclusion says LLMs up to 350B parameters, while Table 1 lists PaLM L as 540B.
record.rows_left_out: Table 5's MT5 results are left out because the flattened layout does not support confident assignment of all values to model and training condition. Table 3's context-length results are left out because context length is not scale or pretraining-loss predictability. Table 2 lattice-quality metrics and the combined-model results are not individual LLM size-sweep outcomes.

untested.parts: No fitted or predictive curve of downstream WER against size, and no link to pretraining loss. Only a qualitative size trend is shown, on ASR rescoring.

missing.what: MT5 XL vs XXL on en-in dev: raw 16.6 vs 16.8; WEBDOC fine-tuned 16.1 vs 16.3. The XL fine-tuned value of 16.1 matches Table 6, supporting this alignment. The larger model is worse.

record.verdict_notes: The Table 4 eval column has 11 values for 12 rows, so eval alignments are uncertain and r15's 'reversed' state is unsupported. The conclusion says 350B parameters, but Table 1 lists PaLM L at 540B. Effects across sizes are tiny (0.1–0.2 WER) and no uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss or power-law fits over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of substantially larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or compute-optimal parameter/token split.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
The study evaluates text-pretrained LMs on ASR rescoring; it does not test whether power laws hold across modalities or training regimes.
Tests downstream WER and salient-term error rates in long-form ASR, not other downstream tasks, a relationship to pretraining loss, or actual predictions of downstream performance.
No scaling-law exponents, compute-optimal split, fitting-method comparison, or curve-bending analysis.

relationships.condition: T5 sizes 60M–11B, en-us dev (and eval up to XL)
relationships.reason: Dev WER falls monotonically from 11.9 to 11.5 with T5 size; eval falls 15.9 to 15.7 (r1, r3, r6, r8, r2, r4, r7).
relationships.display_finding: Development word error rate decreased monotonically from 11.9 to 11.5, while evaluation word error rate decreased from 15.9 to 15.7.

relationships.condition: Largest models: PaLM 62B→540B dev; T5 XL→XXL eval; MT5 XL→XXL en-in dev (Table 5, from text)
relationships.reason: Gains plateau: PaLM L equals PaLM M on dev (r14), and T5 XXL equals XL on eval (r9). Per Table 5 text, fine-tuned MT5 XXL (16.3) is worse than XL (16.1).
relationships.display_finding: PaLM L matched M on development data and T5 XXL matched XL on evaluation data, while fine-tuned MT5 XXL worsened to 16.3 from XL's 16.1.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: T5 size comparisons on en-us dev and eval; PaLM dev and eval through 62B; MT5 XL on en-in; reported salient-term results
reader_labels.reason: WER or STER improves over the first-pass baseline in these reported rescoring settings, though the study does not fit or validate predictive scaling curves (r1-r4, r6-r14, r16-r19).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.reason: The largest tested PaLM has worse eval WER than the 62B model, so downstream improvement is not uniformly monotonic with size in this comparison (r15).
